title: What happened at the close
text: Friday was a rough day for tech. The Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 3.5% to $690.49, and the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 1.8% to $755.77. Chip makers fell hardest: AMD dropped 10.9% to $504.80 and Broadcom fell 5.5%. Eli Lilly went the other way and rose 3.2% to $1,417.54 after its report. A day like this shows why holding many kinds of companies matters. This is for learning, not advice.

title: AMD falls almost 11%
text: AMD closed at $504.80, down 10.9% in one day and 23% below its 52 week high of $658.52. Its price is about 128 times its yearly profit, which is very high, so the stock can swing a lot when mood changes. Our risk score for AMD is 7.5 out of 10, which is High.

title: Chip stocks fall together
text: Broadcom fell 5.5%, TSMC fell 5.9%, Vertiv fell 5.5% and NVIDIA fell 4.2%. When companies depend on the same big idea, here AI spending, they often move as a group. That is the difference between the AI giants (a smaller drop of 1% to 1.6%) and the companies that supply them.

title: Lilly bucks the trend
text: Eli Lilly rose 3.2% to $1,417.54, close to its 52 week high of $1,449.68, after reporting third quarter sales that beat what experts expected. It was the only stock on our board with a big gain, a good example of how different industries can behave differently.

title: Lesson 31: What is a market correction?
text: A correction is when a stock or an index falls at least 10% from its recent high. It is a normal part of investing and happens often, usually every year or two. A drop of 20% or more is called a bear market. The Nasdaq is now about 7.8% below its October high, so it is close to correction territory. Corrections can feel scary, but they are also the price investors pay for growth over many years. A long time horizon, a mix of different investments, and not selling in a panic are the usual tools people use to stay calm.
